content.thinking:
I need to avoid inserting any actual numbers myself, using placeholders like {series_before} and {series_while_broken} instead. The symptom here is latency, not error rate—account pages got slow—so I should describe the latency series rising to a peak using placeholder labels, and be careful not to echo the 1500ms figure from the log verbatim.

For the causal chain: pages were slow because basket-total calls to the pricing dependency (io-pricing) slowed down, with no recorded config changes; a restart of io-pricing coincided with recovery, suggesting degraded internal state was the root cause even though the record doesn't confirm why it degraded. I'll note the timing correlation between the restart and the recovery metrics as supporting evidence without overstating certainty.

I also want to flag process gaps worth addressing: the alert was mislabeled as "error rate" when it was really latency, and it fired roughly six minutes after onset, so detection was both delayed and mislabeled. Action items should cover investigating why io-pricing slowed (prevention), fixing the alert description/adding a proper latency alert on the pricing dependency (detection), and adding a timeout or fallback on basket-total calls (mitigation), plus noting that the proposed code fix doesn't clearly address the actual dependency-side cause.

action_items.item: Investigate why io-pricing slowed on basket-total requests: examine its resource use, logs and state around the onset to find the degradation that the restart cleared.
Add a bounded timeout and a graceful fallback (for example a cached or deferred basket total) to io-shop's call to io-pricing, so a slow pricing service does not slow whole pages.
Add a latency alert on calls from io-shop to io-pricing, and correct the HighLatency alert description so it names latency rather than error rate.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow pages for about {duration}. The latency series behind the alert rose from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average, peaking at {series_at_worst}. The failure rate did not rise: it was {errors_while_broken} against {errors_before} before.
io-shop's latency jumped because its calls to the pricing service for basket totals became very slow. The share of requests hit by slow calls grew from a minority to nearly all of them.

The pricing service (io-pricing) was itself slow, or unreachable in a way that made calls slow. The shop's own code and configuration were unchanged: no production changes and no flag changes preceded the onset.

Restarting io-pricing was followed by a return to baseline, and the paging rule stopped firing. This points at degraded state inside io-pricing. The record does not show what that state was or why it arose, so the chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The cause of the pricing service's slowdown is unknown. The record holds only the restart, which cleared the symptom, so the same degradation could recur.
io-shop appears to wait on slow pricing calls with no tight timeout or fallback, so a slow dependency passed straight through to shoppers as slow pages.

Detection was slow and confusing. The alert was raised only after the slowdown had been under way for several minutes, near its end. It was described as an error-rate alert although the series it evaluates is latency, and nothing watched the pricing dependency directly.
The draft fix pull request (AI-2) is open, but the evidence points at the pricing dependency rather than io-shop code. It is unclear that merging it would prevent a repeat.

input.executive_summary: For about {duration} ({alert_raised} alert, onset {began}) the shop's account pages were much slower than normal. Shoppers' requests mostly still succeeded: the failure rate stayed at its usual level, {errors_while_broken} against {errors_before} before. Page latency rose from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and {series_at_worst} at its worst, so shoppers waited noticeably longer for pages that normally load quickly. The slowness traced to an internal pricing service that the shop calls for basket totals. Argus restarted that service, and the shop was back at baseline from {recovered}. The underlying reason the pricing service slowed is not yet known.

got_lucky: Metrics were back at baseline from {recovered}, in the same minute as the restart. Recovery may have been partly spontaneous, so the restart's effect is not cleanly separated from it.
Shoppers' requests mostly kept succeeding despite the slow dependency, so the harm was delay rather than failed pages.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert within seconds, put the onset at the right minute from the metrics, and tied the latency to the pricing dependency using the logs.
The restart was verified against the metrics before the incident was closed, and there was nothing to put back.
went_wrong: The alert text said error rate while the series was latency, and the failure rate never rose, which could mislead responders.
The root cause in io-pricing is still unexplained, and the alternative candidate C2 was never tried or ruled out.

input.root_cause: The pricing service that io-shop calls for basket totals became very slow, and io-shop waited on every one of those calls, so its pages slowed. The record does not show why the pricing service slowed down. No deploy or flag change preceded it, and a restart of the pricing service was followed by recovery.
